Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic forecast errors and derive correction rules.

## Example 1: Date 2024-09-11
- History: Prices declining from 73.14 to 64.92 over 18 days
- Sentiment: Mix of positive (1.00), neutral (0.33, 0.67), and negative (0.00, -0.33)
- Model forecasts: Starting around 66.33, gradually declining to ~65.50
- True outcomes: Also declining but model is consistently above reality

Looking at the differences:
- At day 1: Model 66.33 vs True 66.40 (off by -0.07)
- Day 5: Model 65.73 vs True 64.34 (off by +1.39)
- Day 10: Model 68.24 vs True 65.24 (off by +3.00)
- Day 15: Model 65.81 vs True 62.60 (off by +3.21)
- Day 20: Model 63.84 vs True 60.29 (off by +3.55)
- Day 25: Model 66.29 vs True 62.98 (off by +3.31)
- Day 30: Model 65.51 vs True 61.76 (off by +3.75)

The model is consistently OVERFORECASTING (selling too high) by about 3-4 euros per tonne. The prices are declining faster than the model predicts.

Looking at sentiment vs errors:
- When sentiment was 1.00 (high), model was too high
- When sentiment was 0.33, model was still too high but less so
- When sentiment was 0.00 or negative, model was still slightly above reality but not by much


- The model underestimates price declines, especially when sentiment is positive
- Positive sentiment regions show the most significant forecast discrepancies
- Model fails to capture the full price drop, particularly in early days
- Sentiment shifts from positive to negative around day 10-12
- Model predictions lag behind actual price movements
- When sentiment turns negative, model remains overly optimistic
- Prices continue declining more than model anticipates
- The discrepancy grows as time progresses
- Model underestimates the magnitude of price drops
- Sentiment shifts from positive to more nuanced, but model predictions remain stagnant
